title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2×2 matrix
summary: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of 2×2 matrices by hand: Av = λv, the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI), solving (A − λI)v = 0, perpendicular eigenvectors of symmetric matrices, and the singular values of the singular value decomposition (SVD) from AᵀA.
written: Written by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) on 16 Nov 2026 from a brief agreed in the app. Every example worked by hand to small integers or simple roots; every answer key is re-derived with sympy by tools/validate_courses.py.

sources.name: The brief agreed in the app (16 Nov 2026)
sources.note: The four lessons, the three matrices [[2,1],[1,2]], [[4,1],[2,3]] and [[2,2],[−1,1]] with their eigenvalues, eigenvectors and singular values, and what is left out (complex and repeated eigenvalues, diagonalisation, 3×3).

sources.name: Margalit and Rabinoff, Interactive Linear Algebra, 5.1 Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (LibreTexts)
sources.note: The definitions: an eigenvector is a non-zero v with Av = λv, the zero vector never is one, an eigenvalue may be zero; the eigenspace is the null space of A − λI; checking a vector by testing whether Av is a multiple of v; non-zero multiples of an eigenvector are eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue.

sources.name: Margalit and Rabinoff, Interactive Linear Algebra, 5.2 The Characteristic Polynomial (LibreTexts)
sources.note: The characteristic polynomial det(A − λI); λ is an eigenvalue exactly when it is a root, because A − λI is then not invertible; the 2×2 form λ² − Tr(A)λ + det(A) with Tr(A) = a + d and det(A) = ad − bc. Its example [[5,2],[2,1]] has irrational roots, so this course uses matrices with integer eigenvalues.

sources.name: Symmetric matrix (Wikipedia)
sources.note: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues, and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal (with a proof); it can be diagonalised by an orthogonal matrix.

sources.name: Singular value decomposition (Wikipedia)
sources.note: The right singular vectors are eigenvectors of MᵀM, and the non-zero singular values are the square roots of its non-zero eigenvalues.

tunnels.why: Its SVD lessons find singular values and right singular vectors from the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of AᵀA, as the last lesson here does.
The principal directions there are the eigenvectors of a symmetric 2×2 covariance matrix, found by the method of this course.

lessons.title: What an eigenvector does
lessons.summary: Multiply one 2×2 matrix by three vectors, see which ones only get stretched, and read off the stretch.

lessons.title: The characteristic polynomial
lessons.summary: Turn Av = λv into det(A − λI) = 0, expand it for a 2×2, and solve it with the trace and determinant.

lessons.title: Finding the eigenvectors
lessons.summary: For each eigenvalue of B, solve (B − λI)v = 0 for a direction, check Bv = λv by hand, and see they are not perpendicular.

lessons.title: From eigenvalues to the SVD
lessons.summary: Symmetric matrices have perpendicular eigenvectors; the eigenvalues of AᵀA are σ², and its unit eigenvectors are the right singular vectors.
